situation:
You are the Marketing Manager and the Brand Manager at GREENFIELD CONSUMER LENDING, a fintech company that makes small personal installment loans to borrowers most banks turn away. The CEO (judge) is a third-generation member of the family that founded the company and has asked to meet with you today about a decision that touches both the company's brand and its legal exposure.

GREENFIELD was started by the CEO's grandfather forty years ago on a simple promise: lend fairly to working people with thin or damaged credit files, at rates lower than payday alternatives. That promise is still the center of every advertisement the company runs, and it is the reason GREENFIELD's customer base skews toward borrowers with below-average credit scores. The company has grown quickly in recent years, adding new borrowers faster than its back-office operations were built to handle.

Growth has outpaced the loan-servicing platform GREENFIELD leases from an outside vendor, which can actively manage no more than 42,000 open accounts before its compliance monitoring becomes unreliable. The portfolio hit that ceiling last month, and every new renewal now means declining someone already on the books. An anonymous whistleblower report reached the CEO (judge) two weeks ago from inside the underwriting department, alleging that renewal decisions have quietly favored the highest-credit-score borrowers, the very customers GREENFIELD's advertising says it does not prioritize.

Keeping the stronger-credit borrowers would lower the portfolio's default rate and protect the reserves GREENFIELD needs to keep lending to anyone at all, including the harder-credit borrowers it takes on next year. Keeping the weaker-credit borrowers instead would honor the promise the brand is built on, but would raise defaults inside a portfolio that is already at its servicing ceiling, and could strain the relationship with the vendor the whole platform depends on. Either path can be defended to a regulator; neither can be defended to every customer.

The CEO (judge) wants the participant team to recommend which group of existing borrowers GREENFIELD should prioritize for renewal under the account ceiling, and how the company should describe that choice publicly without contradicting its own advertising or inviting a claim of unequal treatment. Nothing has been decided or communicated to any customer yet, and the underwriting department is waiting on direction before the next renewal cycle begins.

The CEO (judge) will greet the participant team, ask to hear their recommendation, and ask questions about how it would actually be carried out inside the company, from the underwriting department to the customers who are affected. At the end of the presentation and the questions that follow, the CEO (judge) will thank the participant team for their time and their work.
